content: The Surveillance Guide for Vaccine-Preventable Diseases in the WHO South-East Asia Region: Pertussis Module (September 2023) provides detailed guidance on the surveillance, diagnosis, and management of pertussis (whooping cough). Below is a professional summary of the key points: Introduction The continued high transmission rates of pertussis in many countries highlight the waning immunity provided by acellular pertussis vaccines, necessitating additional booster doses for improved disease control. Low-income countries using whole-cell pertussis vaccines often lack epidemiological data, which is critical for formulating policies on booster doses. Surveillance is essential to understand the epidemiology and control of pertussis. Objectives of Surveillance The primary goals of pertussis surveillance are: 1. Monitoring disease burden and the impact of vaccination programs, with a focus on morbidity and mortality in children under five years of age. 2. Generating data to optimize vaccine schedules and delivery strategies. 3. Guiding public health responses to pertussis outbreaks. Case Detection A suspected pertussis case is defined as any individual with a cough lasting at least two weeks or any duration in infants or outbreak settings, accompanied by at least one of the following symptoms: Paroxysms (fits) of coughing. Inspiratory whooping. Post-tussive vomiting (vomiting after coughing). Apnea (in infants under one year of age). Physicians may suspect pertussis in patients with a cough of any duration, especially in vaccinated or previously infected individuals who may not exhibit classic symptoms. Description of Symptoms Paroxysms of Cough: Frequent, spasmodic bursts of 5–10 coughs in a single expiration, often accompanied by bulging eyes, tongue protrusion, cyanosis, and neck vein distension. Episodes are worse at night and disrupt sleep. Whoop: A rapid inspiratory sound caused by air being drawn in against a closed glottis after a coughing fit. Post-Tussive Vomiting: Vomiting immediately after coughing, sometimes expelling a mucus plug. Other Signs: Response to Suspected Cases Within 24 Hours: Clinicians must notify public health authorities. Within 48 Hours: Public health authorities should investigate the case, collect nasopharyngeal swabs, and initiate treatment without waiting for laboratory results. Close contacts should be identified, and symptomatic contacts should be treated. Specimen Collection Nasopharyngeal swabs should be collected within four weeks of cough onset. Two swabs are ideal: one for culture and one for PCR testing. Throat and anterior nasal swabs should not be used. Specimens must be collected using sterile polyester, rayon, or nylon flocked swabs (not cotton swabs) and transported appropriately. Laboratory Testing Culture: The gold standard for confirming pertussis, though it is less sensitive (<60%) and takes 3–7 days for results. Culture is most successful in infants and within the first two weeks of illness. PCR: More sensitive and faster than culture but prone to false positives and negatives. PCR sensitivity decreases after four weeks of cough onset or after five days of antibiotic treatment. Serology: Useful for cases identified 4–12 weeks after cough onset, particularly in adolescents and adults. However, it is not recommended for children under 10 years or those vaccinated within the past year due to reduced sensitivity and specificity. Case Classification Laboratory-Confirmed Case: A suspected case with laboratory confirmation via isolation of Bordetella pertussis or detection of its genomic sequences by PCR. Alternatively, elevated IgG antibodies to pertussis toxin in individuals aged 11 years or older, one year after the last vaccine dose, can confirm the case. Epidemiologically Linked Case: A suspected case with close contact with a laboratory-confirmed case within three weeks prior to cough onset. Clinically Compatible Case: A suspected case meeting the clinical definition but lacking laboratory confirmation. Discarded Case: A suspected case that does not meet the pertussis case definition. Contact Tracing and Management Close Contact Definition: High-Risk Contacts: Infants, pregnant women in the third trimester, healthcare workers caring for infants or pregnant women, and individuals living or working with infants. Testing: Only symptomatic contacts should be tested. PEP should focus on high-risk groups, including infants, pregnant women in the third trimester, and their close contacts. Vaccination Undervaccinated individuals exposed to pertussis should receive age-appropriate pertussis-containing vaccines. Immunity from natural infection or vaccination wanes over time, necessitating booster doses. Outbreak Management An outbreak is defined as an increase in pertussis cases or incidence above the baseline in a specific area. Confirming the circulation of Bordetella pertussis is critical for an appropriate response. This guide emphasizes the importance of timely diagnosis, treatment, and vaccination to control pertussis and prevent its spread, particularly among vulnerable populations.
